opus-5.5.text:
I think it's going to come from a few places at once, but honestly a lot of it comes from people who are writing kernels day to day and getting frustrated. When we were working on FlashAttention, so much of the effort wasn't the algorithmic idea, it was the plumbing: managing shared memory, figuring out the right tiling, getting the async copies and the tensor core instructions lined up. And every new hardware generation, Hopper, then Blackwell, you basically have to relearn a chunk of that. So the people who feel that pain most acutely are usually the ones who end up building the abstractions.

You can already see that happening. NVIDIA's CUTLASS and CuTe came out of trying to describe layouts and tiling in a composable way, and that layout algebra turned out to be a really powerful idea. Triton came from the other direction, saying most people don't want to think about individual threads, let's let them think in blocks and have the compiler handle a lot of the details. And then there's a newer wave of tile-based languages and DSLs, things like ThunderKittens and others, that try to sit somewhere in the middle: give you the key primitives, like a tile of a matrix in registers or shared memory, without making you hand-write everything.

I'd say the pattern is that good abstractions come from looking at a lot of real kernels and noticing what keeps repeating. Attention, matmul, the various state space and linear attention variants: underneath, they're mostly about moving tiles of data through the memory hierarchy and feeding the tensor cores. If you can name those things well, you get a lot of mileage.

I'm also cautiously optimistic about AI helping here. Not that a model will magically write the perfect kernel tomorrow, but having models that can generate and check lots of kernel variants changes what kind of abstraction you want. Maybe you want something that's easy for both humans and models to reason about and verify.

And academia has a real role too, because companies are often optimizing for their own hardware on a tight timeline, whereas researchers can step back and ask what the right general concepts are. So I think it'll be this mix of practitioners, compiler folks, hardware vendors, and researchers, and the best ideas will probably come out of people who sit at the intersection of the algorithms and the hardware.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's going to come from a few different places, and honestly I think they'll coexist rather than one winning out.

The first is what I'd call the "narrow DSL" direction. The reason CUTLASS and CuTe exist, and the reason we wrote things like ThunderKittens with some of the Stanford folks, is that there's a relatively small set of primitives you actually need for the workloads that matter right now. You need to describe tiles, you need to describe how those tiles move through the memory hierarchy, and you need to describe how they get fed into the tensor cores. If you build an abstraction around those three things, you can cover an enormous fraction of the FLOPs that are actually being spent in the world, and you can get a lot closer to the hardware than a general-purpose compiler can. The tradeoff is that it's opinionated. It's not going to help you write a sort or a graph algorithm.

The second direction is compilers, things in the spirit of Triton, or TVM, or what the XLA and Mojo folks are doing. The pitch there is you write something that looks like Python or NumPy and the compiler figures out tiling and scheduling. I'm honestly more optimistic about this than I used to be, mostly because the hardware vendors are now investing in these directly. Triton being inside PyTorch means NVIDIA and AMD both care about it. The limitation is that every new generation ships with some new feature, like TMA or warp specialization on Hopper, or whatever Blackwell is doing with the tensor memory, and the compiler lags the hardware by a year or two. So the frontier kernels still end up being written by hand.

The third one, which I think people underrate, is the hardware vendors themselves. The abstractions that stick tend to be the ones that match what the hardware actually does. CuTe layouts are a good example. They look weird at first, this whole algebra of shapes and strides, but it's because the hardware really is organized that way, and once you internalize it everything else gets simpler. So I expect a lot of the good abstractions to come out of the people who are co-designing the chip and the software, because they know what the next three generations look like.

And then the thing I'd flag that's new is the models themselves. We're already at the point where you can hand a model a reasonably well-specified kernel problem and it'll produce something that's within some factor of a hand-tuned version. It's not replacing the human yet on the hardest stuff, but what it changes is the economics. Right now the reason we need abstractions is that there are maybe a few hundred people in the world who can write a good attention kernel on a new chip. If that bottleneck loosens, the question of "what's the right abstraction" becomes a bit less urgent, because the cost of just writing the specialized thing goes down. I think the abstractions will still matter, but they'll matter more as a way to make the search space tractable, whether the one doing the search is a person or a model.

So if I had to bet, I'd say the near-term wins come from these narrow, hardware-aware DSLs that a small group of people get really good at, and the longer-term wins come from compilers getting good enough that most people never have to think about it, with models filling in the gap in between.

r001.rationale: The response describes abstractions built around the primitives needed by important workloads and separately says useful abstractions should match the hardware’s capabilities.

r002.rationale: It discusses tensor cores and moving tiles through memory, but does not say that faster matrix multiplication makes overlapping it with other operations more important.

astra-6.text:
My guess is they’ll come from people working closely with both the algorithms and the hardware. You take something like attention, try to make it fast, and discover which details you need to control—how data moves, what stays in shared memory, how you overlap computation with memory access. Then you ask which of those ideas are useful beyond that one kernel.

That’s where a good abstraction can emerge. You want to express the important choices without having to manage every low-level detail yourself. But figuring out what’s important takes experience across a range of workloads. If you abstract too early, you can hide exactly the thing you need to control for performance.

So I expect it to be an iterative process between people writing kernels and people building languages and compilers. Better tools make it easier to experiment with algorithms, and those experiments show us what the tools need to express.

sol-6.1.text:
My guess is they’ll come from people working closely with both the algorithms and the hardware. When you implement something like attention, you discover which details you need control over—how you move data, how you tile the computation, how you overlap communication with compute. Then the challenge is to expose that control without making everyone write all the low-level machinery themselves.

I’m excited about the space between CUDA and a framework like PyTorch. You want to express the algorithm at a fairly high level, but still have a clear way to understand and influence what runs on the GPU. A useful abstraction should make common patterns easy while letting you go deeper when performance requires it.

I think that will be an iterative process: build kernels for real workloads, identify the patterns that keep coming up, and turn those into language and compiler features.
